fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul commands the church to keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life, one "…not in keeping with the tradition you received from us." (2 Thessalonians 3:6). It's a command given in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Nothing in the verse is about questions or travel. It's about how a person is living.

Good guess, but that's not in the verse. The command is about a brother who leads an undisciplined life that isn't in keeping with the tradition they received (2 Thessalonians 3:6). Paul never says anything about asking elders questions here. I bet a lot of bakers would have stamped that one too, and I'd be first in line.

Nope, no suitcases in this verse. The command is to keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life that is not in keeping with the tradition they received (2 Thessalonians 3:6). Travel never comes up. Paul's team is talking about how a brother lives, not where he goes.

Not quite. Nobody in this verse is worried about being a stranger. They worked night and day so they "…would not be a burden to any of you." (2 Thessalonians 3:8). Stranger doesn't even make it into the oven, friend.

That's the one, friend. Paul says they had the right to support, "…but we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate." (2 Thessalonians 3:9). They had the right and chose to work anyway. Talk is cheap, so they showed it with their own hands.

True, friend. Paul writes, "For we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives, accomplishing nothing, but being busybodies." (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Accomplishing nothing is right there in the verse. He says it straight, no sprinkles on top, and it's only some of them.

Teamwork is lovely, and I'd take a crowded kitchen any day. But Paul says to "…begin working quietly to earn their own living." (2 Thessalonians 3:12). The word he picks is quietly, and that's the one that goes in the blank.

That's it, friend. Here Paul speaks to the brothers: "But as for you, brothers, do not grow weary in well-doing." (2 Thessalonians 3:13). Well-doing is the work, and he's telling them not to wear out on it. Keep going.

Slow and steady is a fine habit, but Paul says something else. He writes, "…do not grow weary in well-doing." (2 Thessalonians 3:13). Weary is a word I understand, friend. Years in the back of a junk drawer wore me out too.
